CausalChain: Radiotherapy -> Increased tumor cell death and neoantigen release -> Activation of dendritic cells in draining lymph nodes -> Expansion of precursor exhausted CD8+ T cells in STIE -> Infiltration of these cells into TIME -> High TGF-β1/IDO levels in TIME promote terminal T cell exhaustion -> TGF-β1 blockade prevents exhaustion and sustains a reinvigoratable T cell state -> PD-1 inhibition effectively restores T cell cytotoxicity
Hypothesis: Simultaneous administration of a TGF-β1 inhibitor with radiotherapy and PD-1 blockade will reprogram both the systemic and tumor immune microenvironments by preserving precursor exhausted T cells and preventing their terminal exhaustion, thereby enhancing anti-tumor efficacy and reducing the occurrence of hyperprogression in cancers such as hepatocellular carcinoma and non-small cell lung cancer.
Abstract: The immune landscape of solid tumors is intricately shaped by both the local tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) and the systemic tumor immune environment (STIE). Recent studies have revealed that radiotherapy not only induces tumor cell death and subsequent neoantigen release, but also modulates the balance between various immune regulatory factors, such as TGF-β1 and IDO. These molecules can push infiltrating T cells toward an exhausted state, thus hampering the effectiveness of PD‐1 blockade therapies. We propose a hypothesis that combining TGF-β1 blockade with radiotherapy and PD‐1 inhibitors can reprogram the TIME and STIE to preserve and reinvigorate precursor exhausted CD8+ T cells, mitigating terminal exhaustion and enhancing anti‐tumor immunity. This integrated strategy may be particularly beneficial for cancers with high levels of TGF-β1 such as hepatocellular carcinoma, as well as in situations where hyperprogression is observed after immune checkpoint inhibition.
